11. [Page 14] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) as having an intrinsic nature, based on the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of all phenomena through the causal conditions of mutual dependence, like a dream or a magical illusion. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the realization that the self-nature of false discrimination does not exist within the self-nature of dependent origination, and it is the non-dual state free from the grasping of subject and object. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of the ultimate truth? It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is the sphere of self-realization (*pratyātma-gati*) and is free from the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the notions of existence and non-existence regarding these four kinds of self-nature. Thus it is said: The false, the dependent, the perfected, and the ultimate— These are the four kinds of self-nature taught by the Buddhas. False discrimination is the attachment to names and forms; Dependent origination is the arising of phenomena through causes. When one realizes that the false does not exist in the dependent, That is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. The realm of the Tathāgatas, free from existence and non-existence, Is the self-nature of the ultimate truth, realized within oneself.

— 19 — The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a jasmine flower, and the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells in a village or a town or a city, and he is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. Now, when that person hears, ‘In such-and-such a village or town or city, there is a bhikkhu who is an arahant or one practicing for arahantship,’ he goes to that bhikkhu. Having approached him, he listens to the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gains faith. Having gained faith, he reflects thus: ‘It is not easy for me to live the spiritual life under the Blessed One while remaining in this village or town or city. Then, having taken his belongings, he departs from that village or town or city and goes to where the Blessed One is. Having approached the Blessed One, he pays homage to the Blessed One and sits down at one side. As he is sitting there, the Blessed One instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens him with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a talk on the Dhamma, his mind becomes detached from the things that fetter it and becomes liberated from the taints through non-clinging. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells in a village or a town or a city, and he is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. Now, when that person hears, ‘In such-and-such a village or town or city, there is a bhikkhu who is an arahant or one practicing for arahantship,’ he goes to that bhikkhu. Having approached him, he listens to the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gains faith. Having gained faith, he reflects thus: ‘It is not easy for me to live the spiritual life under the Blessed One while remaining in this village or town or city. But at the time of death, he attains final knowledge. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a jasmine flower? ‘It is not easy for me to live the spiritual life under the Blessed One while remaining in this village or town or city. Then, having taken his belongings, he departs from that village or town or city and goes to where the Blessed One is. Having approached the Blessed One, he pays homage to the Blessed One and sits down at one side. But after the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell. This, monks, is called a person like a fragrant sandalwood tree. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

Just as a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow, though pierced deeply, does not feel pain so long as the arrow-head remains within; but when that arrow-head is extracted, he experiences intense suffering—so too, O King, the mind is bound by the fetters of desire.

99. When the arrow-head has been pulled out, the wound becomes painful; likewise, when the mind is freed from the bonds of craving, it experiences the suffering of separation. 100. One should therefore uproot this craving with wisdom, just as one would pull out a thorn from one’s foot. Page 147: "The Bodhisattva's Resolve" (Bodhicitta) In the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, Śāntideva states: "By the power of this merit, may all beings attain the state of Buddhahood; And until that time, may they never be separated from the thought of awakening. This verse encapsulates the essence of the Mahāyāna path: the generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*). It is not merely a wish, but a commitment to liberate all sentient beings from suffering by attaining the omniscience of a Buddha. This resolve serves as the foundation for the subsequent practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* explains, there are two types of bodhicitta: the conventional (*saṃvṛti-bodhicitta*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha-bodhicitta*). The former is the aspiration born of compassion, while the latter is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) inseparable from that compassion. Together, they form the dual nature of the path. Furthermore, the process of stabilizing this resolve involves both the "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) and the "application" (*prasthāna*) aspects. The vow is the formal pledge to follow the path, while the application is the actual engagement in the practices that fulfill that pledge. Through these two, the bodhisattva traverses the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), gradually purifying their mind and accumulating the two collections of merit and wisdom.
Thus, the cultivation of bodhicitta is the very heart of the Mahāyāna tradition, transforming an ordinary being into a vessel capable of achieving the highest goal for the sake of all who suffer.

PAGE 880 The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when those who have not yet heard this Dharma hear it, they will experience a state of joy and rapture. They will think: ‘We have obtained great gain; we have met with a great friend. Ānanda, this Dharma discourse is a great Dharma discourse, a discourse that brings about the destruction of all suffering. It is a discourse that leads to the cessation of craving and to the realization of Nirvāṇa. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse? How should it be remembered? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, this Dharma discourse is called ‘The Great Compassion of the Tathāgata,’ and it should also be remembered as ‘The Discourse on the Destruction of All Suffering. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed for the forest grove. There, the Blessed One sat upon a prepared seat and addressed the monks: “Monks, I shall teach you the Dharma discourse known as ‘The Lamp of the Tathāgata. Listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “Even as a lamp, monks, dispels the darkness of night and illuminates the world, so too does this Dharma discourse dispel the darkness of ignorance and illuminate the path to liberation. It is a teaching that reveals the nature of reality, a teaching that leads to the transcendence of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. Sitting there, he addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many qualities must a monk possess to be established in the fruit of Arhatship? The Blessed One replied: “Kāśyapa, a monk must possess five qualities to be established in the fruit of Arhatship. What are these five? First, he must be free from attachment to sensory pleasures. Second, he must be free from malice toward sentient beings. Third, he must be free from dullness and torpor. Fourth, he must be free from restlessness and remorse. Fifth, he must be free from doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Kāśyapa, a monk who possesses these five qualities is established in the fruit of Arhatship. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said: “Blessed One, wonderful is this teaching! Most wonderful is this teaching! It is as if the Blessed One were to turn upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden. It is as if he were to show the way to one who is lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes may see forms. Even so has the Blessed One taught the Dharma in various ways. I take refuge in the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

441. “The Blessed One has said: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are those four? They are: the person who goes from darkness to darkness; the person who goes from darkness to light; the person who goes from light to darkness; and the person who goes from light to light. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “From darkness to darkness one goes, And from darkness to greater darkness; From darkness to light one goes, And from light to greater light. One who is possessed of faith, virtue, and wisdom, Who is learned and free from stinginess, Having abandoned both darkness and light, From light to light one goes. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? Herein, monks, a certain person dwells pursuing the practice of body-contemplation in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells pursuing the practice of feeling-contemplation in feelings... the practice of mind-contemplation in the mind... the practice of phenomena-contemplation in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and dejection regarding the world. “Monks, when a noble disciple dwells thus, practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, he is said to be one who is walking upon the path that leads out of the world, one who is treading the path of the Dhamma, one who has set out toward the right direction, and one who is not a mere follower of the crowd. “Just as, monks, when a cowherd with eyes leads a herd of cattle across a fordable river, he does not lead them by force, nor does he let them go where they please; rather, he leads them step by step across the ford. So too, monks, when a noble disciple dwells thus, practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, he is said to be one who is walking upon the path that leads out of the world, one who is treading the path of the Dhamma, one who has set out toward the right direction, and one who is not a mere follower of the crowd. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “The four foundations of mindfulness, Developed and cultivated, Lead to the complete destruction of suffering. When a noble disciple dwells thus, Practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, He is said to be walking upon the path, Treading the path of the Dhamma. He has set out toward the right direction, And is not a mere follower of the crowd. Like a cowherd leading cattle Across a fordable river, He leads them step by step To the further shore of suffering. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? The person who goes from darkness to darkness; the person who goes from darkness to light; the person who goes from light to darkness; and the person who goes from light to light. “And how, monks, is a person one who goes from darkness to darkness? Herein, monks, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of caṇḍālas, hunters, bamboo-workers, cart-makers, or scavengers—poor, with little food and drink, where life is hard to maintain, and where clothing and food are obtained with difficulty. And he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he is short-lived, often sick, and dull-witted. He does not gain access to the Ariyan disciples’ teachings. Having no access to the teachings, he does not understand the meaning of those teachings that have been well-expounded by the Teacher or by his disciples. “He practices in such a way that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a place of perdition, even in hell. This, monks, is called a person who goes from darkness to darkness. “And how, monks, is a person one who goes from darkness to light? Herein, monks, a certain person is reborn in a low family... [as above] ...and he is dull-witted. He does not gain access to the Ariyan disciples’ teachings. Having no access to the teachings, he does not understand the meaning of those teachings that have been well-expounded by the Teacher or by his disciples. “But he practices in such a way that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. This, monks, is called a person who goes from darkness to light. “And how, monks, is a person one who goes from light to darkness? Herein, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or householders—rich, with great wealth and property, abundant in gold and silver, with many treasures and granaries, and many possessions.

And he is handsome, attractive, and fair to look upon; he is long-lived, seldom sick, and intelligent. He gains access to the Ariyan disciples’ teachings. Having access to the teachings, he understands the meaning of those teachings that have been well-expounded by the Teacher or by his disciples. “But he practices in such a way that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a place of perdition, even in hell. This, monks, is called a person who goes from light to darkness. “And how, monks, is a person one who goes from light to light? Herein, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family... [as above] ...and he is intelligent. He gains access to the Ariyan disciples’ teachings. Having access to the teachings, he understands the meaning of those teachings that have been well-expounded by the Teacher or by his disciples. “He practices in such a way that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Page 107: "The Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Perfection of Wisdom" (Prajñāpāramitācaryā) [The Bodhisattva] practices the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). He does not perceive form (*rūpa*) as real, nor does he perceive feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as real. He does not perceive the eye (*cakṣus*) as real, nor does he perceive the ear (*śrotra*), nose (*ghrāṇa*), tongue (*jihvā*), body (*kāya*), or mind (*manas*) as real. He does not perceive form (*rūpa*) as real, nor does he perceive sound (*śabda*), odor (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*), or mental phenomena (*dharma*) as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajā vedanā*) as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) as real, nor does he perceive the water element (*abdhātu*), fire element (*tejodhātu*), wind element (*vāyudhātu*), space element (*ākāśadhātu*), or consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) as real. He does not perceive ignorance (*avidyā*) as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*), the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the limitless (*atyantaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of the beginningless and endless (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāraśūnyatā*), the emptiness of nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-characteristics (*alakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of inherent nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*), or the emptiness of the non-existence of inherent nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*) as real. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as real, nor does he perceive the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), or the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) as real. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as real, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive stages of cessation (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), or the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*) as real. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) as real, nor does he perceive the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), or even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) itself as real. Why is this? Because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are non-arisen and non-ceased. Since they are thus empty, they cannot be apprehended. This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom through non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should train himself in this way: "I shall purify the Buddha-fields, yet I do not perceive a Buddha-field as real. "I shall mature sentient beings, yet I do not perceive sentient beings as real. "I shall realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet I do not perceive that enlightenment as real. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom. By practicing thus, he is said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm him. Just as a man who has entered the womb of a lioness cannot be harmed by any other animal, so too, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom in this way cannot be overcome by Māra or the hosts of Māra. For what reason? Because he has entered the domain of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Subhūti, just as a king’s son who has been anointed and invested with the royal insignia cannot be intimidated by any of the ministers or officials, so too, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom in this way cannot be intimidated by any of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, this is the supreme practice of the perfection of wisdom for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. By practicing this, he quickly attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and, having attained it, he will never fall back from the state of a Bodhisattva. He will swiftly reach the stage of non-retrogression and, after passing through the various stages, he will finally attain the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, Subhūti, you should train yourself in this way: "Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have practiced the perfection of wisdom, so shall I practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is the instruction for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom.

150. "The Blessed One has taught that there are three kinds of feeling: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. This is what was said. However, it was not stated by the Blessed One that these feelings are exclusively internal; rather, they were taught as being both internal and external. Furthermore, it was not stated that these feelings are exclusively worldly; rather, they were taught as being both worldly and supramundane. Nor was it stated that these feelings are exclusively conditioned; rather, they were taught as being both conditioned and unconditioned. It was also not stated that these feelings are exclusively mundane; rather, they were taught as being both mundane and supramundane. And it was not stated that these feelings are exclusively with outflows; rather, they were taught as being both with outflows and without outflows. Therefore, since the Blessed One did not teach that these feelings are exclusively internal, exclusively worldly, exclusively conditioned, exclusively mundane, or exclusively with outflows, one should understand that the Blessed One did not intend for them to be taken in such a way. Contact, mental volition, and consciousness are taught by the Blessed One as being both internal and external, both worldly and supramundane, both conditioned and unconditioned, both mundane and supramundane, and both with outflows and without outflows. Therefore, since the Blessed One did not teach that these nutriments are exclusively internal, exclusively worldly, exclusively conditioned, exclusively mundane, or exclusively with outflows, one should understand that the Blessed One did not intend for them to be taken in such a way. XX. Procedure for Vrata Observance [Page 34] 1. Having performed the preliminary rites (pūrvāṅga) such as the purification of the site (bhūmiśodhana), the drawing of the mandala (maṇḍalalekhana), and the invocation of the deities (devatāvāhana), one should prepare the sacrificial ground. 2. The officiant (ācārya), having purified himself through ritual bathing (snāna) and wearing clean garments, should enter the sanctified area while reciting the purificatory mantras. 3. One should then perform the rite of the five fires (pañcāgnisādhana) and offer oblations (homa) according to the prescribed rules, using clarified butter (ājya) and other sacrificial materials. 4. The practitioner (sādhaka) should observe the vows (vrata) with a focused mind, maintaining silence (mauna) and celibacy (brahmacarya) throughout the duration of the observance. 5. At the conclusion of the rite, one should perform the final offerings (tarpaṇa) and the distribution of gifts (dakṣiṇādāna) to the preceptor and the assembled assembly. 6. By following this procedure, the practitioner attains the fulfillment of all spiritual goals and the grace of the deities.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas and the great multitude of śrāvakas: "If there are sentient beings who wish to invoke the Great Peacock King, they should first perform the following ritual: They should take a clean cloth, seven cubits long and four cubits wide, and have it dyed with saffron. Upon this cloth, one should draw the image of the Great Peacock King. His body shall be golden in color, adorned with various precious ornaments. He shall have two wings, each possessing five hundred eyes, and his tail shall be spread out like a canopy. On his head, he shall wear a jeweled crown, and from his mouth shall issue a thousand tongues of fire. Beneath his feet, he shall trample upon a great serpent king. To the left and right of the image, one should draw the images of the eight great nāga kings, all of whom are holding incense burners and offering them to the Great Peacock King. Furthermore, one should draw the images of the four great heavenly kings, each holding a white lotus flower and standing in attendance before the Great Peacock King. Having completed the drawing of these images, one should then prepare a clean altar, sprinkle it with perfumed water, and scatter various flowers upon it. One should place fragrant lamps at the four corners of the altar and offer various kinds of food and drink. Then, facing the image of the Great Peacock King, one should sit in the lotus position, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and circumambulate the image three times. After performing this ritual for seven days and seven nights, one will surely see the Great Peacock King manifesting his true form and bestowing blessings and protection. The Buddha told the great assembly: "If there are sentient beings who wish to invoke the Great Peacock King, they should diligently practice this ritual without negligence. If they do so, they will obtain immeasurable merit and be free from all calamities and obstacles. Thus spoke the Buddha. All the great bodhisattvas and the great multitude of śrāvakas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and carried it forth. 38 The Chapter on the Ritual for Offering Food. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas and the great multitude of śrāvakas: "If there are sentient beings who wish to offer food to the Great Peacock King, they should first prepare various kinds of pure food and drink, as well as various fruits and delicacies. They should place these offerings before the image of the Great Peacock King and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. After reciting the mantra, they should visualize the Great Peacock King receiving the offerings and partaking of them. By performing this ritual, one will cause the Great Peacock King to be satisfied and grant the practitioner immeasurable blessings and protection. The Buddha told the great assembly: "If there are sentient beings who wish to offer food to the Great Peacock King, they should diligently practice this ritual without negligence. Regarding "pagamyena" and so forth—422–423. [The text continues with the following: If one were to say that the self (ātman) exists because it is perceived by the mind, this is not tenable. For the mind does not perceive the self as a distinct entity; rather, it perceives only the aggregates (skandhas). Furthermore, since the mind is momentary and lacks continuity, it cannot serve as a basis for the perception of a permanent self. Moreover, if the self were perceived by the mind, it would follow that the self is impermanent, just like the mind itself. Therefore, the self does not exist as a real entity. As for the argument that the self exists because there must be an agent for the experience of pleasure and pain, this too is untenable. Pleasure and pain arise from specific conditions, such as contact between the sense organs and their objects; there is no need to postulate a separate agent. If the self were the agent, it would have to be either eternal or non-eternal. If eternal, it could not be the cause of changing states like pleasure and pain. If non-eternal, it would be subject to arising and ceasing, and thus could not be a permanent self. Consequently, the self is merely a conceptual construct (prajñapti) based upon the aggregates. Thus, the self is not found to exist apart from the aggregates, and the notion of a self is a mental fabrication. This concludes the refutation of the self according to the Abhidharma principles.

It is considered pure and conducive to spiritual merit, provided it is not obtained through improper means or with excessive persistence. This mode of subsistence is prescribed for those who have renounced worldly attachments and seek liberation. By partaking of such food, one remains free from the bonds of greed and attachment, thereby facilitating progress on the path toward ultimate truth. It is said that even the gods sustain themselves on such alms when they descend to the mortal realm. Thus, the consumption of alms-food is a traditional practice that purifies the mind and body alike. It is particularly recommended for ascetics and those living in the forest hermitage, as it ensures a life of simplicity and detachment from material possessions. Through this discipline, one cultivates contentment and equanimity, which are essential virtues for the seeker of dharma. Therefore, the wise advocate the acceptance of alms as a means of sustaining life while maintaining spiritual integrity. This practice is rooted in ancient tradition and is praised as a source of purity and self-restraint. Consequently, those who follow this way of life are regarded as true practitioners of dharma, devoted to the welfare of all beings. In this manner, the consumption of alms-food serves as a vital support for the cultivation of inner virtues and the realization of the supreme goal. O Kṛṣṇa, on the northern path, one who is restrained in mind should bathe the god, the dispeller of darkness, with ghee, milk, and other such substances.
Having properly worshipped with offerings of beautiful garments, flowers, incense, and unguents, and then likewise with the thorough honoring of the Brahmins;
Devoted to the Sun, one should properly undertake the vow of two steps;
O lord of men, one should worship Citrabhānu while bathing, likewise while eating,
and likewise while walking after having eaten, [all] to Citrabhānu.
Whether sleeping or awake, he should always perform the fire-oblation as well as worship.
I shall perform the chanting of the names of the Sun daily,
from this day forward, until the commencement of the southern solstice.
I shall always act in this manner and proclaim the Lord of the World;
likewise, I shall never speak an untruth or any harsh word against the Supreme Self.
Whether out of ignorance or knowledge, I shall proclaim the Lord;
one should indeed recite [the mantra] of Citrabhānu for six months at most.
Remembering him at the time of death, may I go to whatever destination he attains;
may that same destination be mine, even if my death should occur within six months from now.
Therefore, I have here offered my own self to Bhāskara;
for even the Supreme Self, Brahmā, is ultimately composed of Citrabhānu.
Remembering Yaśasvin, that Sun is my supreme goal;
whether at dawn, at evening, or at midday, O best of kings,
if the vow consisting of this renunciation has been performed within six months, O King.
*Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, Brāhma-parvan, 108, 7–25.
O Lord of the World, refuge of all people, act in such a way that [the world] may be free from suffering.
"O Citrabhānu, just as my refuge comes from you according to the proper rule," having uttered this, he observed the vow dedicated to Citrabhānu for six months.
One should cause them to be winnowed until the arrival of the southern solstice;
then one should perform that propitiation of the Fire-god according to one's ability.
One should feed divine and terrestrial Brahmins along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
and likewise recount stories of the meritorious souls in the presence of Mārtaṇḍa.
O Lord of the Earth, one should worship the reciter with devotion according to one's ability;
O Kṛṣṇa, that man who thus causes this vow to be recited—
Or a woman, O tiger among gods, is liberated from all sins;
even if their death should occur within six months, they are freed.
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever fruit is proclaimed for fasting, that he attains; there is no doubt in this, for your lotus feet are always worshipped by one who is truly devoted.
In ancient times, Bhānu sang this *Citrabhānupavadvandra-vrata*, which destroys all sins, to Bhava when he was questioned by Kṛṣṇa.

Now, the vows lasting for a year;
[first, the Sārasvata vow].
"O King, you have asked rightly; listen to the Sārasvata vow, by the mere recitation of which Sarasvatī is pleased in this world."
Whatever man devoted to me may perform this unsurpassed vow,
he should do so by first worshipping a Brahmin at the beginning of the year.
Alternatively, on a Sunday, with the strength of the planets and lunar mansions,
one should feed the Brahmins milk-rice (pāyasa) after performing the ritual recitation by the Brahmins.
Having given white garments along with gold according to one's ability,
one should worship Gāyatrī with devotion using white garlands and unguents.
O Goddess, just as the Blessed One, the Grandfather of the world of Brahmā,
would not remain after abandoning his own [nature], so do you become a bestower of boons.
O Goddess, may I never be deprived of all the Vedas and Shastras, nor of dance, song, and the like; likewise, may the Siddhis be mine.
O Sarasvatī, protect me with these eight forms: Lakṣmī, Medhā, Varā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Sṛṣṭi, Prabhā, and Mati.
Having thus worshipped Gāyatrī— who is adorned with a lute-neck,
who possesses a water-pot, and who desires nourishment— with white flowers and unbroken rice grains, one should do so with devotion.
One who knows the Dharma should eat in silence at both morning and evening;
and on the fifth day of each fortnight, one should worship Chandravāsinī.
*Matsyapurāṇa*, Chapter 66, Verses 3–18; *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, Uttaraparvan, Chapter 35, Verses 3–19.
Likewise, in the Kṛtyakalpataru, it is stated: "One should give a prastha of rice together with a vessel of clarified butter,
milk, and gold, saying, 'May Gāyatrī be pleased.'"
Likewise, one should practice silence during the twilight hours;
no food should be consumed in between for as long as thirteen months.
Upon the completion of the vow, one should give a meal consisting of sesame seeds and rice,
a full water-pot, a pair of garments, and a beautiful cow to a Brahmin.
And for the Goddess, [he should offer] a canopy with a bell, accompanied by white eyes and feet;
sandalwood, a pair of garments, betel-nut, and again a pinnacle.
Likewise, one should worship the teacher who instructs with devotion,
free from stinginess regarding wealth, using garments, garlands, and ointments.
Whoever performs the Sārasvata vow according to this procedure becomes possessed of learning, wealth, and prosperity.
Thus ends the Sarasvata-vrata in the Matsya Purāṇa.

1. Matsya Purāṇa – Chapter 11, Verses 1–14. [Page 473] The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter Eleven, verses one through fourteen, begins as follows: 1. O best of Brahmins, I shall now describe to you the supreme and most excellent *Matsya Purāṇa*, which is the foremost among all the Purāṇas. 2. This Purāṇa contains one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses; it is the first of all the Purāṇas and is known as the *Matsya*. 3. It is the source of all the Purāṇas and is the very essence of the Vedas. It is the origin of all the worlds and the supreme means for attaining liberation. 4. In this Purāṇa, the creation of the world, its dissolution, and its maintenance are described in detail, along with the genealogies of the patriarchs and the reigns of the Manus. 5. Herein are found the histories of the kings, the duties of the various social orders (*varṇas*), the stages of life (*āśramas*), and the rules for the performance of sacrifices. 6. The science of astronomy, the art of statecraft, the methods of warfare, the secrets of alchemy, and the means of attaining longevity are also revealed here. 7. The worship of the gods, the propitiation of the ancestors, the rites for the departed spirits, and the various forms of penance are all explained in this work. 8. The characteristics of the different ages (*yugas*), the decline of dharma, the rise of adharma, and the ultimate restoration of righteousness are all set forth. 9. The nature of the soul, the path of transmigration, the fruits of karma, and the means of attaining the supreme goal are clearly elucidated. 10. This Purāṇa is a treasure-house of knowledge, containing all the mysteries of the past, present, and future, and it grants both worldly prosperity and spiritual liberation. 11. Having heard this Purāṇa, which is like a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, one is freed from all sins and attains the highest state. 12. This is the secret of all the gods, the essence of the Upaniṣads, and the foundation of all sacred traditions; it should be recited with devotion by those seeking merit. 13. By listening to this Purāṇa, one gains wisdom, long life, health, and prosperity; it destroys all misfortunes and leads to the fulfillment of all desires. 14. Therefore, O best of sages, listen with a focused mind to this *Matsya Purāṇa*, for it is the supreme means for attaining all goals of human existence.

3 [page 514–to–514] “O King, you have been born as a human being through the power of your own merit; therefore, do not abandon this human body. For one who has attained a human birth, there is no other state more difficult to find than this. O King, you have obtained a human existence that is exceedingly rare in the world. Therefore, do not cast it away; rather, strive to attain the supreme goal. The king replied: “I am indeed a human being, but I am suffering from the affliction of leprosy. My limbs are falling apart, my body is covered in sores, and I am tormented by intense pain. What purpose would there be for me in remaining alive? The physician said: “O King, do not despair. There is a medicine that can cure even such a disease as this. It is found in the Himalayas, but it is extremely difficult to obtain. It is called ‘Vaidūrya-ratna’ (Lapis Lazuli Gem). If one obtains it and applies it to the body, all diseases will be destroyed and one will become free from illness. The king asked: “How is that medicine to be obtained? Where does it grow, and what are its characteristics? The physician replied: “It grows on the slopes of the Himalayas at a place where the sun’s rays never reach. Its color is like the clear sky, and it possesses a radiance that dispels all darkness. It is surrounded by various medicinal herbs and protected by divine beings. One must go there with great care and fetch it. The king said: “If that medicine exists, I shall go myself to fetch it, even if I must traverse the entire earth. I cannot bear to remain in this state of suffering any longer. Thus, out of compassion for his subjects and desiring to benefit them, the king resolved to seek the supreme medicine. He summoned his ministers and counselors and declared his intention. Having prepared his chariot and gathered his retinue, he set out toward the Himalayan mountains, accompanied by his physicians and attendants. [page 515] Upon reaching the mountain range, the king and his party searched diligently for the Vaidūrya-ratna. After many days of wandering through dense forests and scaling steep cliffs, they finally reached the sacred grove where the jewel was said to grow. There, amidst the fragrant herbs and the presence of celestial beings, they beheld the radiant gem, shining with a light that surpassed the brilliance of the sun. The king, filled with joy, took the jewel and returned to his capital. Once there, he had the medicine ground into a fine powder and applied it to his body. Immediately, his leprosy vanished, his skin became smooth and golden-hued, and his health was fully restored. The king then ruled his kingdom with righteousness, bringing happiness to all his subjects. Thus, through the power of perseverance and the grace of the Dharma, even the most grievous of ailments can be overcome. Therefore, one should never lose heart when facing adversity, but should always strive to cultivate virtue. [End of page 514]
